newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-DECADES PASS BUT JUVENTUS REMAIN CONSTANT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DECADES PASS BUT JUVENTUS REMAIN CONSTANT.

text.p: While world soccer has changed beyond recognition over the past century, Juventus have remained constant. The current Italian champions just keep on winning.
The Turin-based club, which celebrates its centennial on November 1 this year, won its first Italian title in 1905 with a side containing a mixture of poets, painters and factory workers.
In those days, soccer goalposts did not have nets attached and the Juventus goalkeeper of the time, Luigi Durante, used to protest vigorously when a goal was awarded against him.
Durante would argue that the ball had not really passed between the posts and would rush to the sidelines to shout: "I appeal to the people".

If the current Juventus goalkeeper Angelo Peruzzi concedes a goal in Wednesday's Champions Cup final against German side Borussia Dortmund, he is more likely to confine his appeal to his defensive team mates.

With 24 Italian titles, two Champions' Cups, three UEFA Cups, one Cup Winners' Cup, two Intercontinental Cups and nine Italian Cups on their sideboard, Juventus are not only Italy's most successful club but also the best supported.
Following a dispute with the firm which administers Turin's city owned Stadio Delle Alpi, Juventus recently threatened to abandon their native city.

Juventus were prepared to play league and Cup games in cities all over Italy from Palermo in Sicily to Trieste on the border with Slovenia, confident that wherever they go, they will command a full house.
The name Juventus is forever linked with that of Agnelli, the family which controls the destiny of Italian car giant FIAT.

Since the early '20s, a member of the Agnelli family has been involved in day-to-day Juventus affairs while for most of this century the club has been owned either by Istituto Finanzaria Industriale (IFI), the vast Agnelli-owned holding company, or directly by FIAT itself.
Founded as the Sport Club Juventus in 1897, the side now famous all over the world for its black and white strip began its playing days in a curious strip of pink shirts and black bow ties.

When Juventus play a centennial celebration friendly against English side Newcastle United in Cesena on August 3, it will be the visitors who line up in black and white while Juventus will don a pink shirt in memory of that first ever side.
Legend has it that the fate of Juventus was irrevocably changed by a left-back called Antonio Bruna.
Bruna was a FIAT factory worker and Juventus team player of the early '20s who got involved in a row with the factory foreman when he asked for time off for special training with the team.
In the end, the argument reached the ears of Giovanni Agnelli, the man who in July 1899 had founded the Fabbrica Italiana di Automobili Torino (FIAT).
The FIAT boss not only allowed Bruna time off to train but he also encouraged his son, Edoardo, to take a direct interest in the affairs of Juventus.

From that moment on, success seemed guarranteed for Juventus, so much so that the club has become a byword to Italians for style, elegance and title wins and earned itself the nickname, "La Vecchia Signora", the Old Lady.

In the immediate post-war period, Giovanni Agnelli's grandson, Gianni, entered the Juventus board room in 1947 as an enthusiastic 26-year-old determined to stamp his mark on his much loved family club.

Gianni Agnelli did just that, getting personally involved in the purchase of a long line of class players such as Giampiero Boniperti, Swede John Hansen, Argentine Omar Sivori, Welshman John Charles in the '50s right through to perhaps his favourite of all, Frenchman Michel Platini in the '80s.

Agnelli, known as "L'Avoccato" or The Lawyer, has often maintained close personal contacts with his favourite players, sometimes phoning them early in the morning to hear their views on the previous day's game.
During one season, he promised Boniperti a cow for every goal he scored.

"Boniperti is a good administrator. That year he won himself a lot of cows and, above all, the farm foreman always complained because everytime he went to claim his cow, he picked one that was in calf", Agnelli said.
Gianni Agnelli also had the perspicacity to appoint Giampiero Boniperti club president from 1971 to 1990, a period when the club won seven Italian titles.
Currently Juventus are guided by a trio comprising former player now vice-President Roberto Bettega, managing director Antonio Giraudo and coach Marcello Lippi.
Bettega, Giraudo and Lippi have masterminded a Juventus comeback, winning the 1995 title after a nine-year break.

That title win and last year's Champions Cup triumph against Dutch side Ajax Amsterdam signalled loud and clear that Juventus had emerged from the uncustomary shadows of a decade when Italian and world soccer was dominated by their great rivals, AC Milan, winners of five Italian titles and three Champions Cup between 1988 and 1996.

The manner in which the Bettega-Giraudo-Lippi team have been able to sell off champions such as Roberto Bettega, Fabrizio Ravanelli and Gianluca Vialli in recent seasons and yet find more than adequate replacements bears witness to their skill.

The evolution this season of 22-year-old Nicola Amoruso and 24-year-old Christian Vieri in attack and of 24-year-old Frenchman Zinedine Zidane in midfield suggests new chapters are about to be written in the Juventus success story.
Perhaps, the next chapter starts in Munich on Wednesday.
